"Your mother compared me to your cousin's wife again," Omkar said, dropping onto the bed. "At lunch. In front of everyone."

"I know," Tushar said. "I heard."

"I've been holding it in for weeks. I go quiet at their house and then I'm cold with you at home." Omkar paused. "I'm not saying your parents are bad. I'm saying I feel small when it happens."

Tushar sat up. "I hadn't seen how much it lands. Thank you for not just... going cold."

"What can we do?"

"I can say something the next time. Not an argument, just, 'Please don't compare.' And we could spend less time at those big lunches."

"That I can do," Omkar said.

qa.q: What did Tushar's mother compare Omkar to?
qa.a: She compared Omkar to Tushar's cousin's wife.

qa.q: How does Omkar say the comparisons feel, and what has it been causing at home?
qa.a: Omkar says they make Omkar feel small, and the bottled-up feeling has made Omkar go quiet at the parents' house and cold with Tushar at home.

qa.q: What did Omkar do well that others could learn from?
qa.a: Omkar spoke to Tushar without attacking the parents, saying "I'm not saying your parents are bad," and asked what they could do together about boundaries.

qa.q: How might Tushar have felt hearing Omkar's complaint?
qa.a: Tushar probably felt a mix of discomfort and gratitude: Tushar admitted not having seen how much it lands and thanked Omkar for speaking up instead of going cold.

grounding: Shows quietly resenting a partner's family for comparing them to others, sharing it with the partner without attacking their parents, and agreeing boundaries together.

Sunday, first week of June. At lunch in Ketaki's parents' house, her mother passed Raghav the dal and said, "Vishal got a car from his company. Such a go-getter." Raghav smiled with his teeth. On the drive home he answered Ketaki in single words. At night he lay awake, listing every comparison since the wedding.

Wednesday. Ketaki put her tea down. "You've been cold for three days. Is it me?" He almost said nothing. Then: "It's not you. When your mother compares me with Vishal, I feel measured and never enough. And when they drop in without calling, I feel invaded. I've been swallowing it." She was quiet. "I didn't know it hurt that much."

Two Sundays later. They had agreed: visits on weekends, with a call first, and Ketaki would speak to her mother herself. At lunch, when Vishal's name came up, Raghav just asked about his new job, and meant it.

qa.q: What had Vishal got from his company?
qa.a: Vishal got a car from his company.

qa.q: What was Raghav feeling on the drive home that Sunday?
qa.a: Raghav felt resentful and hurt, measured against Vishal, and it leaked out as cold single-word answers.

qa.q: Why did Raghav's Wednesday talk with Ketaki work?
qa.a: He described his own feelings without attacking her parents, which let them agree on boundaries together.

qa.q: How did Ketaki experience Raghav's coldness before he explained?
qa.a: She was confused and worried, even asking whether it was her fault.

grounding: The story shows a man quietly resenting his partner's family for comparison and intrusion, then sharing it without attack and agreeing on boundaries together.

passage:
You keep saying "fine" about your in-laws, Trisha, and your face says something else. So let your Vinita maasi tell you what "fine" cost me.

When I married, your uncle's family lived two floors down. My mother-in-law came up every evening, opened my pots, and said, "Kamla's daughter-in-law makes softer rotis." I said nothing. For eleven years, nothing. But I stopped laughing when she laughed. I found reasons to be busy when they came. Your uncle thought I simply disliked his family.

One night he asked why I had gone so cold. I nearly shouted, but I didn't blame his mother. I told him, "I feel inspected in my own kitchen." He was shocked. Together we asked that visits be on Sundays. It helped. But eleven years of silence had already put ice between us that took long to melt. Don't wait eleven years.

qa.q: What did Vinita's mother-in-law compare her with?
qa.a: She compared her with Kamla's daughter-in-law, who made softer rotis.

qa.q: How did young Vinita feel during those silent years?
qa.a: She felt resentful and inspected in her own kitchen, and it came out as coldness rather than words.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Vinita's story?
qa.a: When her husband asked why she had gone cold, she described her own feeling without blaming his mother, and they agreed on Sunday visits together.

qa.q: How did Vinita's husband see her coldness before she spoke?
qa.a: He simply thought she disliked his family, because her silence gave him no other explanation.

grounding: An elder's story shows how bottled resentment toward in-laws leaks out as coldness, and how sharing it without attack led to boundaries agreed together.
